svg.text: FIVE STRICTLY LINEAR PHASES — RoundState enum, one way only
no cards on the table yet
never gets a turn at all.
BUST is terminal for that seat, but
the ROUND keeps going for the others.
no per-seat state classes — one enum + one cursor ✓
resolve(player) — first match wins, top to bottom:

g.text: a bust loses even if the dealer busts too
every surviving seat wins at once

svg.text: resolve() is PURE — no money, no strategy, no mutation. Fully unit-testable on its own. ✓
then: netPayout(bet, outcome) → new RoundResult(name, outcome, bet, net) · state = DONE

g.text: WHY AN ENUM, NOT STATE CLASSES?
Five transitions, all one-way, none of them
branching. A GoF State hierarchy would mean
five classes each implementing six methods,
at the top of each method does the same job
in one line, and fails fast with the phase name.
If every seat already busted the dealer draws
nothing and returns an empty list — the
outcome is already decided, and burning cards
would change the next shoe deal for no reason.
REPRODUCIBILITY & THREADING — the two questions that always come
All randomness sits behind one seeded Random created inside Deck.shuffled(seed) / Shoe.of(n, seed). Same seed → identical
deal, every run. Tests use fully scripted Deck.of(card, card, ...) so no assertion ever depends on chance.
Threading: there is none, deliberately. One table = one round loop; seats act in strict turn order, so there is no shared
mutable state to guard and no lock anywhere in the codebase. Scale by running many independent tables, each confined
to its own thread — the Blackjack object is the confinement boundary.
Say this out loud rather than adding synchronized to look careful — unjustified locking is a red flag too.

g.text: Phases: BETTING → PLAYER_TURN → DEALER_TURN → SETTLEMENT → DONE (no backward edge)
Guarded by requireState() · seeded · single-threaded by design — LLD
